Hidden in a shelter beside the De Lacey cottage, he watches Felix, Agatha, and their blind father treat one another with care. He gathers firewood for them at night and learns words from their conversations. Safie's arrival brings regular language lessons that he follows from hiding. Reading and observation give him a knowledge of history, morality, family, and property, while also making the absence of companionship in his own life increasingly painful.

The creation speaks privately to blind De Lacey and is received calmly, but Felix returns and beats him before hearing his explanation. The family soon leaves the cottage. In despair and anger, the creation burns their abandoned home. A later attempt to save a drowning child ends with him being shot. He travels to Geneva, kills William after discovering his connection to Victor, and plants evidence on Justine. He now asks Victor to make a female companion who will share his exile, promising that both beings will disappear into a remote wilderness. Victor fears the request but accepts, reasoning that a companion may end the violence and remove his creation from humanity.

Victor accompanies Clerval to Britain and separates from him to work on an isolated Scottish island. While constructing a female being, he imagines the danger that she may refuse the promised exile or that the pair may reproduce. He tears the unfinished body apart while the first creation watches. The being promises to be present on Victor's wedding night. After disposing of the remains at sea, Victor lands in Ireland and is detained for murder. The dead man is Clerval, killed by strangulation. Victor becomes dangerously ill, then is acquitted when evidence establishes that he was elsewhere at the time of the killing. His father takes him back toward Geneva, but Victor tells him nothing of the threat.

Victor and Elizabeth marry. Expecting the creation to attack him, Victor sends Elizabeth away while he searches their lodging, leaving her unprotected. The creation kills her and escapes. Alphonse dies after learning of the murder, and Victor asks the authorities to hunt the being, without success. He follows his enemy across Europe and Russia and onto the Arctic ice, sustained by supplies and messages the creation leaves to prolong the chase. characters.name: Hans Van Ripper

recaps.text: Centuries after a devastating war, the One State encloses its city behind a Green Wall and regulates its citizens through the Table of Hours. People have numbers instead of names, live in glass buildings, and lower their blinds only for officially authorized sexual visits. D-503, the mathematician directing construction of the spacecraft Integral, begins a written record that will travel aboard it and persuade other worlds to accept the One State's exact happiness. He is proud of a society that treats freedom as a primitive source of error. His familiar companions are O-90, one of his assigned partners, and the state poet R-13. During a walk he meets I-330, whose mockery and confidence unsettle him. She takes him to the Ancient House, a surviving opaque building filled with objects from private life, and seems to disappear through it. D knows he should report her conduct but hesitates.

D-503's encounter with I begins to disturb both his timetable and his sense of himself. He dreams, an experience the One State regards as a symptom, and becomes preoccupied with irrational mathematics and with the hairy hands that connect him to the human past he despises. I arranges meetings outside the ordinary rules, uses alcohol and tobacco, and obtains medical excuses through a cooperative doctor. D follows despite alternating between desire, fear, and the intention to denounce her. A Guardian, S-4711, appears repeatedly near them, making it impossible for D to tell whether the authorities already know about I. The more D tries to translate his reactions into equations, the more he encounters an inner division that official language cannot settle. His record, intended as praise of perfect order, becomes evidence that he can no longer experience that order as complete.

I-330 draws D further into prohibited privacy. Their meetings at the Ancient House and in D's apartment create absences and lowered blinds that his building supervisor U notices. D experiences jealousy, longing, and rage, while O-90 sees that his attention has shifted away from her. A doctor tells him he has developed a soul, naming individuality as though it were a disease. D attempts to approach the Bureau of Guardians but repeatedly fails to make a clean confession, partly because the watchful S-4711 remains impossible to interpret. The Integral continues toward its test flight, so D's public role as a model engineer increasingly conflicts with his secret conduct. He still repeats the State's principles, yet the diary now records sensations and images that resist them, and he begins to value the very uncertainty he once believed had been eliminated.

D's divided life intensifies. He waits desperately for I, invents explanations for her absences, and discovers that exclusive love cannot be reconciled with the One State's impersonal schedule of partners. O asks him for a child even though the State has not authorized her for motherhood, placing another human desire against official arithmetic. D is horrified by the danger but cannot dismiss her wish. Public preparations continue for the Day of Unanimity, the annual ceremony in which citizens are expected to renew the Benefactor's rule without meaningful choice. R-13 contributes poetry to the State's rituals, while U watches D with a mixture of suspicion and possessive concern. D's work on the Integral remains technically ordered, but he can no longer keep his emotional transformation outside the ship or outside his record.

The Day of Unanimity breaks the appearance of universal consent. When the prescribed public vote is held, I and many others raise their hands against the Benefactor, and the ceremony collapses into violence and confusion before the regime reasserts control. D is caught between fear of the rebellion and his need to find I. She finally reveals that she belongs to the Mephi, a resistance movement connected to people living beyond the Green Wall. Through hidden passages in the Ancient House, D reaches the world outside and encounters uncaged nature and people whose bodies and lives have not been standardized. The Mephi want the Integral for their uprising and need D's position to take it. His love for I and his newly awakened self draw him toward the plot, even as he fears that she may value him chiefly as a means of reaching the ship.

The State answers spreading disorder by announcing the Great Operation, a compulsory procedure that removes imagination and therefore the capacity for inward rebellion. Citizens are urged and then forced to submit. The Mephi prepare to seize the Integral during its flight, with D expected to help deliver the ship. Meanwhile O is pregnant by D in defiance of the State's reproductive rules. I arranges for her to escape beyond the Green Wall, preserving the child at the cost of separating O from D. Street unrest grows as the regime hunts resisters and the boundary between the controlled city and the outside world weakens. D remains committed to I and the planned mutiny, but his uncertainty about surveillance and betrayal persists as the Integral's flight approaches.

The Mephi attempt to take the Integral, but the plan has been reported and the mutiny fails. Rebellion nevertheless spreads through the city, and an explosion breaches the Green Wall, allowing people, animals, and uncontrolled nature to enter. D is captured before he can remain with the insurgents. The Great Operation removes his imagination, ending the divided consciousness his diary has traced. Now loyal without emotional conflict, he gives the Benefactor information about I and the conspiracy. I is arrested and tortured in front of him; she refuses to betray the Mephi, while the operated D observes her suffering without love or pity. O has escaped beyond the Wall carrying D's child. Fighting continues in part of the city, so the regime's victory is not complete. D closes his account convinced that the One State must win because its truth is mathematically certain, unaware that this certainty has been purchased by destroying the self that learned to question it.
